profiles.title: Feedback
profiles.canonical_definition: A circular causal or informational relation in which an output or consequence affects later input, state or action. The sign, delay, reference condition and mechanism must be stated.
profiles.summary: Feedback is not merely receiving comments. It is a circular relation in which consequences return to influence what happens next. The loop may counteract change, reinforce it, oscillate, delay response or fail because no actor can use the returned information.
profiles.why_it_matters: Systems work often says feedback when it means reporting, evaluation, data or learning. Those are only feedback when they close a loop that can alter subsequent action. Sign, delay, reference condition and response capacity determine what the loop actually does.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["negative or balancing vs positive or reinforcing feedback", "feedback vs feedforward", "feedback signal vs capacity to respond", "physical causal loop vs returned information", "feedback mechanism vs homeostatic condition", "measurement vs learning"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["Maxwell 1868: mathematical governor analysis as a precursor", "Black 1934: stabilised negative-feedback amplifiers", "Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow 1943: purposive behaviour and negative feedback", "Wiener 1948: cybernetic synthesis across animals and machines"]
profiles.logical_antecedents: ["distinguishable input, output and state", "a return path through which consequences can alter later conditions", "time, delay and loop gain", "a reference or viability condition where correction is claimed"]
profiles.dependent_subsequents: ["control and regulation", "system dynamics", "management cybernetics", "learning-loop metaphors", "homeostatic and adaptive models"]
profiles.practice_connections: ["ask what information returns to whom", "test whether anyone can alter action in response", "state the delay before effects become visible", "separate balancing from reinforcing loops", "look for loops that reward gaming rather than purpose"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["more feedback is always better", "positive means good and negative means bad", "a dashboard is feedback even when nobody can act", "homeostasis and feedback are synonyms", "all loops stabilise"]
profiles.open_checks: ["Nyquist and Bode lineage", "Forrester and system dynamics", "Bateson, Argyris and learning", "Beer and organisational feedback channels"]
profiles.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

profiles.title: Regulation
profiles.canonical_definition: A relation among disturbances, a reguland, a regulator and acceptable outcomes in which outcome variety is constrained relative to a stated goal or essential-variable range.
profiles.summary: Regulation is the work of keeping outcomes within acceptable ranges despite disturbance. It may operate through feedback, anticipation, constraints, buffering, redundancy, local autonomy or changes to the environment.
profiles.why_it_matters: Regulation is often collapsed into command and control. Ashby instead asks what variety of disturbance reaches the system, what responses are available and which outcomes count as acceptable. The regulator may be distributed rather than a boss or central unit.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["regulation vs domination", "regulator vs manager", "acceptable range vs one fixed target", "distributed vs central regulation", "regulation vs optimisation"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["physiological regulation and governor analysis predate cybernetics", "Wiener connected control and communication", "Ashby formalised regulation in terms of variety and outcomes"]
profiles.logical_antecedents: ["disturbances", "a reguland or essential variables", "acceptable outcomes", "responses and constraints", "information about relevant differences"]
profiles.dependent_subsequents: ["law of requisite variety", "good regulator theorem", "homeostasis", "management cybernetics", "control design"]
profiles.practice_connections: ["identify the variable that must remain viable", "map disturbance variety before adding controls", "ask where regulatory intelligence already sits", "protect local discretion where it carries necessary variety"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["regulation means bureaucracy", "the regulator must be central", "tighter control always improves regulation", "one target captures viability"]
profiles.open_checks: ["legal and institutional regulation as a distinct lineage", "distributed regulation cases"]
profiles.editorial_note: Readable orientation and evidence-backed first pass. Not accepted scholarly consensus until named review is recorded.

nodes.label: Feedback
nodes.description: A family of circular causal or informational relations in which consequences return to influence later state or action. Its sign, delay, reference condition, mechanism and response capacity must be stated.
nodes.canonical_definition: A circular causal or informational relation in which an output or consequence affects later input, state or action. The sign, delay, reference condition and mechanism must be stated.

nodes.label: Regulation
nodes.description: The constraint of possible outcomes under disturbance in relation to specified goals, essential variables or acceptable states. Regulation can use feedback, feedforward, structure, constraint or combinations of them.

sources.title: On Governors
sources.notes: James Clerk Maxwell, Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, vol. 16, pp. 270–283. Bibliographic records span 1867–1868. Used here as a historical precursor to mathematical analysis of governors and control; it does not use the later cybernetic vocabulary of feedback.

sources.title: Behavior, Purpose and Teleology
sources.notes: Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow, Philosophy of Science 10(1), pp. 18–24. Primary pre-cybernetics article connecting purposive behaviour with input/output relations and negative feedback.

sources.title: Cybernetics or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine
sources.notes: Norbert Wiener's foundational synthesis, first published in 1948. The MIT Press open-access reissue describes feedback and information as central to the field. Exact chapter-level use remains a next editorial check.

evidence.excerpt_or_summary: Ashby derives the law as a bound on regulation and states that only variety in the regulator can force down variety due to disturbances.

evidence.locator: International Journal of Systems Science 1(2), abstract and pp. 89–97
evidence.excerpt_or_summary: The paper proves, under stated assumptions, that the simplest optimal regulator is a model of the system in a mapping sense.

evidence.locator: Sections: What Is Feedback?; Negative and Positive Feedback
evidence.excerpt_or_summary: Defines feedback as routing output back to input and distinguishes negative feedback that counteracts deviation from positive feedback that reinforces change.
Maxwell gives a mathematical analysis of centrifugal governors and their stability. The relation is recorded only as a historical precursor to later feedback/control analysis.
The paper treats negative feedback as central to an important class of purposive or teleological mechanisms.
